report.title: The 2026 AI Index Report — Economy chapter

figures.title: Private AI investment by country
figures.subtitle: Total private investment into AI and machine learning companies that have raised over $1.5 million since 2013, top 15 countries, 2025
figures.quote: Global private investment in AI by geographic area, 2025
figures.note: Underlying data is Quid's investment database, not Stanford's own. It counts private financing events only — venture capital and private equity — so it excludes state money. The chapter says explicitly that this understates China: government guidance funds are estimated to have put $184 billion into Chinese AI firms between 2000 and 2023, none of which appears here. Investment is capital committed, not capital spent or value created.

figures.title: AI funding events by deal size
figures.subtitle: Count of global private AI investment events in each size band, 2024 compared with 2025
figures.quote: Global AI private investment events by funding size, 2024 vs. 2025
figures.note: Counts deals, not dollars, so a band with many events can still carry little capital — the report notes the average event was $66.5 million in 2025 and that most dollars flowed through a small number of deals. Quid data; excludes 324 events in 2025 (209 in 2024) whose size was undisclosed, which is why these bands sum to less than the stated totals of 5,505 (2025) and 3,538 (2024).

figures.title: Organizations using AI in at least one business function, by region
figures.subtitle: Share of survey respondents worldwide saying their organization uses AI in at least one function, 2023, 2024 and 2025
figures.quote: AI use by organizations in the world, 2023–25
figures.note: McKinsey & Company's State of AI survey, reproduced by the AI Index — self-reported and not a random sample of firms. A respondent saying their organization uses AI somewhere is not evidence of AI being used at scale: the same survey shows most organizations are still experimenting or piloting rather than fully scaled. Respondent mix changes between waves, so year-over-year moves are directional.

figures.title: AI use by business function in the technology sector
figures.subtitle: Share of technology-sector respondents reporting AI use in each business function, 2025
figures.quote: AI use by industry and function, 2025
figures.note: One row of an eight-industry heatmap from McKinsey's survey, reproduced by the AI Index; technology is the highest-adopting industry, so these are an upper bound rather than a typical firm. Self-reported use in a function, with no measure of depth or of how many people in that function actually use it. Other industries in the same figure run far lower — manufacturing use, for instance, is 9% even inside technology firms.

figures.title: Job postings requiring AI skills, by country
figures.subtitle: AI-skill postings as a share of all job postings tracked in each country, 2025
figures.quote: In 2025, Singapore led with 4.69% of all job postings that required AI skills, followed by Hong Kong (3.5%), Luxembourg (3.4%), and Spain (3.3%). The United States reached 2.6%, followed by Chile (2.4%) and the United Kingdom (1.9%).
figures.note: Underlying data is Lightcast's job-postings database, not an official labour statistic. It measures advertised demand, not hires or filled roles, and coverage of online postings varies by country — a small labour market with a heavily online job board will look more AI-intensive than one where hiring happens off-platform. The report also warns that historical posting counts get revised. Eleven countries shown here; the full series is split across two charts.

figures.title: Job postings requiring AI skills, by US sector
figures.subtitle: AI-skill postings as a share of all job postings in each US sector, 2024 compared with 2025
figures.quote: AI job postings (% of all job postings) in the United States by sector, 2024 vs. 2025
figures.note: Lightcast job-postings data reproduced by the AI Index; sectors are two-digit NAICS codes. This is advertised demand, not employment — a sector can raise its AI-posting share while shrinking overall, and the share rises if total postings fall even when AI postings are flat. The ten largest sectors by 2025 share are shown; the full chart has fifteen, the smallest being waste management at 0.46%.

figures.title: Headcount cuts attributed to AI: observed versus expected
figures.subtitle: Share of respondents reporting an AI-driven decrease in employees over the past year, against the share expecting one over the next year, by business function, 2025
figures.quote: Actual vs. expected change in workforce size as a result of AI by function
figures.note: McKinsey survey data reproduced by the AI Index. The past-year figures are recollection and the next-year figures are expectation — neither is payroll data, and firms have consistently expected more disruption than has arrived. The chapter states that large-scale job losses have not yet shown up in overall employment data. Ten of the eleven functions in the figure are shown; strategy and corporate finance (12% observed, 28% expected) is omitted.

figures.title: Measured change in worker productivity from AI tools
figures.subtitle: Effect sizes from six controlled studies of workers using AI on the job, by occupation, published 2025–26
figures.quote: Customer support agents using a conversational AI assistant resolved 14%–15% more issues per hour (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025), software developers using GitHub Copilot completed 26% more pull requests (Cui et al., 2025), and marketing teams using multimodal AI for ad creation saw a 50% increase in output per worker (Ju and Aral, 2025).
figures.unit: % change in the study's productivity measure
figures.note: Six separate academic studies collected in one AI Index table — not a common measure, so the bars are not strictly comparable. Each measures something different: output volume for authors, completed pull requests for developers, issues resolved per hour for support agents, task speed for the METR study. The -19% METR result is a speed penalty for experienced open-source developers that the same team could not replicate later. A seventh row, customer support agents at +14%–15%, is a range in the report and is left out rather than picking a point value.
